statement: A mobile tool that turns a walk around a car into structured evidence: ten survey areas, defects with photos, and a record the whole marketplace trades on.
team: Product designer; the number of inspectors and the wider team are not recorded in the files
heroCaption: The inspector's app: the survey dashboard with pass and fail counts per area, the inspection queue, and the tyre and body checklist.

snapshot.problem: Dealers bid on cars they never see, so the inspection is the product's evidence. A physical, variable walk-around had to come out as a consistent record.
snapshot.role: Product designer on the inspection app: the queue, the car-details wizard, the area checklists, defect entry and photo capture.
snapshot.result: 27 mobile frames and three local component sets. The files record no field use, inspector count or timing data.

context.heading: The evidence behind every bid
body: On Carsparency a dealer buys a car without seeing it. What they trust instead is the inspection: a Carsparency inspector's record of the car's condition, printed on every detail page in the dealer app and in the report the business hands over.
The inspection app is where that record is made. Its file holds 27 mobile frames, three local component sets and a benchmark page of another inspection app kept for reference.

problem.heading: A walk around a car does not arrive in order
body: An inspector works standing next to the car, on a phone, and no two cars are the same: equipment differs, and a company car has a different title holder from a private one. Yet what comes out has to be comparable from one car to the next.
The design problem is to impose a structure the inspector can follow in any order, without forcing them to type what they can tap, and without letting a skipped area pass unnoticed.

flow.heading: From the queue to a completed record
body: The inspector starts from a queue split into All, In Progress and Inspected. Each card says whether the car is ready to start or already half done, so interrupted inspections are picked up with Continue rather than restarted.

A short wizard captures the car's identity first. Then a dashboard opens the ten survey areas as tiles, each showing how many checks failed and passed, with a time-remaining bar and a single Complete inspection action at the bottom.

solution.heading: Tap what is normal, document what is not
body: Inside an area, each part is a row with a pass and a fail button. A default value is recorded when no defect is reported, so the inspector only spends time on exceptions.

A defect opens its own controls, one toggle each for hail damage, painted, partly repainted, dent, scratch and replaced, and every one that is switched on asks for a description and its own photos. Pictures are taken against named slots (front driver alloy, rear passenger corner and so on), so the photo set is complete and comparable rather than a camera roll.
bullets: Queue: all, in progress and inspected, with search and empty states
Car details: mileage band, title holder, GCC specification, colour, keys and location
Ten areas: car body, transmission, engine, chassis, suspension and brakes, tyres, interior and electrical, air conditioning, glass and mirrors, features
Evidence: per-defect photos, named photo slots, images and videos

ecosystem.heading: The inspection becomes the report, and the report becomes the listing
body: The inspection sits between the seller's own account of the car and the dealer's bid. The seller answers the same questions on the web (title holder, finance, warranty, service history), and the inspector's app verifies them in the field.

What the inspector records flows out twice: into the Advanced Inspection Report, whose defects page uses the same exploded car map as the dealer app, and into the condition sections dealers read in Pro before they bid.

decisions.heading: Four decisions that fit the job to a phone
decisions.lede: Read from the frames; the file shows the choices, not the discussion behind them.

items.title: A dashboard of areas instead of one long form
items.why: An inspector does not walk a car in a fixed order. Ten tiles, each with its own failed and passed counts, let them work in any order and see at a glance what is left.
items.alternatives: A single scrolling form, which punishes any change of order.

items.title: Record exceptions, not everything
items.why: Each part has a default value that stands unless a defect is reported. Most parts of most cars are fine, so the inspector's time goes to the ones that are not.
items.tradeoff: A careless inspector can pass a part without looking; the per-area counts make that visible afterwards rather than preventing it.

items.title: Every defect carries its own proof
items.why: A scratch with no photo is an opinion. Each defect type opens its own description and photo slots, so the report a dealer reads is evidence rather than a checklist.

items.title: Make interruption safe
items.why: Cards in the queue show In Progress and Continue, and the dashboard keeps a time-remaining bar in view. An inspection that stops for a phone call resumes where it stopped.

items.title: Structure is what makes field data comparable
items.body: The value of an inspection is that two cars can be compared. Named slots, fixed areas and fixed defect types do more for that than any amount of free text.

items.title: Design for the exception
items.body: A default value per part keeps the common case to one tap and saves the inspector's attention for the parts that need it.

items.title: A tool used standing up needs to survive interruption
items.body: Resumable inspections and a visible time bar matter as much in the field as any individual screen.
